lessons.title: Evaluating Wool Breeds
lessons.body: Wool breeds are sheep kept mainly for their fleece. In Africa, the most common wool breeds are Merino, Rambouillet, and their crosses. Merino sheep produce fine wool (18â24 microns) that sells for premium prices. They are suited to dry, temperate areas like the Karoo in South Africa or the highlands of Kenya. A mature Merino ewe gives 3â5 kg of greasy wool per year. Rambouillet is a larger, hardier Merino type that does better in colder, higher-rainfall areas. When evaluating a wool breed, first look at the fleece: it should be dense, soft, and free of kemp (coarse hair). Part the wool on the shoulder and sideâyou want a uniform crimp (waviness) and no dark fibres. Second, check the sheepâs body condition: wool breeds should have a body condition score of 3 out of 5 (ribs easily felt but not visible). Third, inspect the mouth for jaw defects and the feet for rot. In Africa, wool is often a secondary product unless you have a market that pays for quality. Shear once a year before the rains. Store wool in dry, ventilated bagsânever in plastic, which causes mould. For smallholders, a good option is to cross a local fat-tailed ewe with a Merino ram to get a dual-purpose animal that gives some wool and good meat. Remember: wool breeds need extra feed for wool growth, so only keep them if you can provide supplementary hay or silage in the dry season. Record fleece weight and quality each year to select the best wool producers.

lessons.title: Evaluating Meat Breeds
lessons.body: Meat breeds are judged by how quickly they grow and how much saleable meat they carry. In Africa, popular meat breeds include Dorper, Suffolk, Hampshire Down, and local fat-tailed breeds like the Blackhead Persian and Red Maasai. Dorper is a South African breed that thrives in arid areas; it sheds its wool, so no shearing needed. A Dorper lamb can reach 35â45 kg live weight in 100â120 days on good pasture. Suffolk and Hampshire Down grow fast but need better feed and care. When evaluating a meat breed, look at the loin eye areaâyou can feel the muscle beside the spine; it should be wide and firm. The hindquarters should be full and rounded. Avoid sheep with narrow, flat rumps. Check daily gain by weighing lambs at birth, 30 days, and 90 days. A good meat breed lamb gains 200â300 g per day. Also assess feed conversion: how many kg of feed to produce 1 kg of gain? Efficient breeds need 4â5 kg feed per kg gain. In Africa, local breeds often have lower growth but are more resistant to worms and heat. A practical strategy is to cross a local ewe with a Dorper or Suffolk ram to get fast growth and hardiness. Keep records of birth weight, weaning weight, and 90-day weight. Select rams from high-growth lines. Provide clean water and mineral licks. Rotate pastures to reduce worms. Meat breeds need a marketâcheck if local butchers pay for weight or carcass quality. If not, focus on local breeds for household meat and sell surplus live animals.

lessons.title: Evaluating Dairy Breeds
lessons.body: Dairy sheep are milked for cheese and yoghurt. In Africa, the main dairy breeds are Awassi, Assaf, and East Friesian. Awassi is a fat-tailed breed from the Middle East, well adapted to dry areas; ewes give 200â400 litres per lactation (180â210 days). Assaf is a cross of Awassi and East Friesian, giving 300â600 litres. East Friesian is the highest producer (500â800 litres) but needs cool climates and high feed. When evaluating a dairy breed, look at the udder: it should be well attached, with two functional teats (not four), and no lumps. Feel the udder for mastitisâhard quarters mean infection. Check the eweâs body condition: dairy sheep should be lean but not thin (BCS 2.5â3). A good dairy ewe has a calm temperament and lets down milk easily. Milk yield peaks 3â4 weeks after lambing. Test milk yield by hand-milking once a day and recording volume. In Africa, dairy sheep are often kept near towns where cheese sells. You need a milking stand, clean buckets, and a cooling tank. Feed lactating ewes 1 kg concentrate per 1 litre milk plus good hay. Without extra feed, milk yield drops fast. Cross local ewes with Awassi or Assaf rams to improve milk without losing hardiness. Select ewes that lamb easily and have twins. Record daily milk yield per eweâcull those below 0.5 litres per day. Remember: dairy sheep need shade and water. In hot areas, milk in early morning. Sell milk to local cheesemakers or make your own yoghurt.

lessons.title: Dual-Purpose Breeds
lessons.body: Dual-purpose breeds give both meat and wool, or meat and milk. They are ideal for African smallholders who need multiple income streams. Common dual-purpose breeds include Romney Marsh (meat and wool), Corriedale (meat and medium wool), and local crosses like Dorper x Merino. In Africa, the best dual-purpose option is often a crossbred ewe: local fat-tailed (for hardiness) crossed with a Dorper (for meat) or a Merino (for wool). When evaluating a dual-purpose breed, set your priorities. If you want more meat, select for growth rate and muscling. If wool matters, select for fleece weight and quality. You cannot maximise bothâa sheep that grows fast may produce less wool. A practical balance: aim for a 40â50 kg mature ewe that gives 2â3 kg wool and weans a 25 kg lamb at 90 days. Check the sheepâs overall conformation: good legs, sound mouth, and a healthy udder. Test wool by parting the fleece; it should be free of kemp. For milk, check udder size and teat placement. Dual-purpose sheep need moderate feedâmore than local breeds, less than pure dairy. In dry seasons, supplement with crop residues (maize stover, groundnut haulms) and mineral blocks. Rotate grazing to control worms. Record birth weight, weaning weight, fleece weight, and milk yield if milking. Select rams from dual-purpose lines. Many African farmers succeed with a three-way cross: local x Dorper x Merino. Keep the best ewe lambs for replacements. Sell surplus males at 6â8 months. Dual-purpose sheep reduce risk: if wool prices fall, you still have meat; if meat prices fall, you have wool or milk.

lessons.title: Selecting Breeding Stock
lessons.body: Selecting the right breeding stock is the most important decision on a sheep farm. Start with your goal: meat, wool, milk, or a mix. Then choose animals that fit your environment and market. For meat, select rams and ewes with fast growth, good muscling, and sound feet. For wool, select for dense, fine fleece. For milk, select for udder quality and milk yield. Always buy from a reputable breeder or a government stationânot from a market where health status is unknown. When selecting a ram, check: testicles (two, firm, equal size), mouth (teeth aligned, no overshot or undershot jaw), legs (straight, no swayback), and fleece (no kemp). A good ram should be at least 12â18 months old and weigh 60â80 kg for meat breeds. For ewes, select those that lamb easily, have good mothering instincts, and produce twins. Avoid ewes with prolapsed vagina or bad udders. In Africa, local breeds are hardy but slow-growing; cross with improved rams to get hybrid vigour. Buy rams every 2â3 years to avoid inbreeding. Keep a ram-to-ewe ratio of 1:25 to 1:40. Record each animalâs ID (ear tag), birth date, parentage, and performance. Cull any ewe that fails to lamb twice in a row, has mastitis, or produces low-weight lambs. Select replacement ewe lambs from your best 20% of ewes. Weigh all lambs at birth, 30 days, and 90 days. Keep only those above average. In hot climates, select for heat tolerance and worm resistanceâuse FAMACHA to check anaemia. Never keep a ram that is aggressive or difficult to handle. Good selection takes time but pays off with a healthier, more productive flock.

lessons.title: Record Keeping for Breed Improvement
lessons.body: Record keeping is the backbone of breed improvement. Without records, you cannot tell which sheep are best. Start with a simple notebook or a smartphone app. Each sheep needs a unique IDâuse ear tags with numbers. Record for each animal: birth date, sex, birth weight, dam ID, sire ID, and birth type (single, twin). At 30 days, record weight and health treatments. At 90 days (weaning), record weight and fleece weight if wool breed. For dairy, record daily milk yield for each ewe. For all, record lambing date, number of lambs born alive, and mothering ability (score 1â5). Use a simple form: one page per ewe per year. At the end of the year, calculate: average birth weight, average 90-day weight, lambing rate (lambs per ewe per year), and fleece weight. Select replacement ewes from dams with above-average lambing rate and weaning weight. Select rams from sires with high growth and good fleece. Cull ewes with two consecutive failures to lamb or low milk. In Africa, many farmers use a wall chart or a ledger book. If you have a phone, use a free app like âLivestock Managerâ or âFarm Recordsâ. Share records with your vet or extension officer. Keep records for at least 5 years to see trends. Remember: you cannot improve what you do not measure. Even a simple tally of lambs born and weaned per ewe will double your flockâs productivity in 3â4 years. Train your family to record daily. Store records in a dry place. Use the data to decide which rams to buy and which ewes to cull. This is how you build a better flock.

quiz.q: Which wool breed is known for fine wool (18â24 microns) and is suited to dry, temperate areas?
quiz.explanation: Merino sheep produce fine wool and thrive in dry, temperate climates like the Karoo.

quiz.q: What is a key sign of a good wool fleece when evaluating a sheep?
options: B) Uniform crimp and no dark fibres
quiz.explanation: A good fleece has uniform crimp and is free of dark fibres and kemp.

quiz.q: How much greasy wool does a mature Merino ewe typically produce per year?
quiz.explanation: A mature Merino ewe produces 3â5 kg of greasy wool annually.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common meat breed in Africa that sheds its wool and thrives in arid areas?
quiz.explanation: Dorper is a South African meat breed that sheds wool and is adapted to arid conditions.

quiz.q: What daily weight gain is expected from a good meat breed lamb?
quiz.explanation: A good meat breed lamb gains 200â300 g per day.

quiz.q: When evaluating a meat breed, what should you check beside the spine?
quiz.explanation: The loin eye area should be wide and firm, indicating good muscling.

quiz.q: Which dairy sheep breed gives 500â800 litres per lactation but needs cool climates?
quiz.explanation: East Friesian is the highest producing dairy breed but requires cool climates and high feed.

quiz.q: How many functional teats should a good dairy ewe have?
quiz.explanation: A good dairy ewe should have two functional teats, not four.

quiz.q: What is a sign of mastitis when checking a dairy eweâs udder?
quiz.explanation: Hard quarters in the udder indicate mastitis infection.

quiz.q: How much concentrate should a lactating dairy ewe receive per litre of milk?
quiz.explanation: Feed 1 kg concentrate per 1 litre of milk produced.

quiz.q: Which of these is a dual-purpose breed known for both meat and wool?
quiz.explanation: Romney Marsh is a dual-purpose breed used for both meat and wool.

quiz.q: What is a practical balance for a dual-purpose ewe in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Aim for a 40â50 kg mature ewe that gives 2â3 kg wool and weans a 25 kg lamb at 90 days.

quiz.q: Why are dual-purpose breeds good for smallholders?
options: B) They reduce risk by providing multiple products
quiz.explanation: Dual-purpose breeds reduce risk because if one product price falls, the other still provides income.

quiz.q: What is a recommended three-way cross for African farmers?
options: A) Local x Dorper x Merino
B) Suffolk x Hampshire x Awassi
C) East Friesian x Assaf x Rambouillet
D) Merino x Rambouillet x Corriedale
quiz.explanation: A three-way cross of local, Dorper, and Merino combines hardiness, meat, and wool.

quiz.q: When selecting a ram, what should you check regarding his testicles?
quiz.explanation: A good ram should have two firm, equal-sized testicles.

quiz.q: What is the recommended ram-to-ewe ratio for breeding?
quiz.explanation: A ram-to-ewe ratio of 1:25 to 1:40 is recommended for breeding.

quiz.q: How often should you buy new rams to avoid inbreeding?
quiz.explanation: Buy new rams every 2â3 years to avoid inbreeding.

quiz.q: Which ewes should be culled from a breeding flock?
options: B) Those that fail to lamb twice in a row
D) Those with high milk yield
quiz.explanation: Cull ewes that fail to lamb twice in a row, have mastitis, or produce low-weight lambs.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of using FAMACHA in selection?
options: B) To check anaemia from worms
quiz.explanation: FAMACHA is used to check anaemia caused by internal parasites like worms.

quiz.q: What is the first step in record keeping for breed improvement?
options: B) Giving each sheep a unique ID
quiz.explanation: Each sheep needs a unique ID, such as an ear tag number, to start record keeping.

quiz.q: Which of these should be recorded for each lamb at birth?
options: A) Birth weight, dam ID, sire ID
quiz.explanation: At birth, record birth date, sex, birth weight, dam ID, sire ID, and birth type.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool for record keeping mentioned for farmers with smartphones?
options: B) Free apps like âLivestock Managerâ
quiz.explanation: Free apps like âLivestock Managerâ or âFarm Recordsâ can be used for record keeping.

quiz.q: How long should you keep records to see trends?
quiz.explanation: Keep records for at least 5 years to see trends in flock performance.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of recording lambing rate?
options: A) It helps select ewes with high fertility
quiz.explanation: Recording lambing rate helps identify and select ewes with high fertility.

quiz.q: Which of these is a key performance record for a dairy ewe?
quiz.explanation: For dairy ewes, record daily milk yield to select high producers.

quiz.q: What should you do with a ewe that has two consecutive failures to lamb?
options: D) Sell her as a dairy ewe
quiz.explanation: Cull ewes with two consecutive failures to lamb to improve flock productivity.

quiz.q: What is the recommended body condition score for a wool breed?
quiz.explanation: Wool breeds should have a body condition score of 3 out of 5 (ribs easily felt but not visible).

quiz.q: Which breed is a cross of Awassi and East Friesian?
quiz.explanation: Assaf is a cross of Awassi and East Friesian, giving 300â600 litres per lactation.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of local fat-tailed breeds in Africa?
options: B) Resistance to worms and heat
quiz.explanation: Local fat-tailed breeds are more resistant to worms and heat than improved breeds.

quiz.q: When selecting replacement ewe lambs, from which ewes should you choose?
quiz.explanation: Select replacement ewe lambs from your best 20% of ewes based on performance records.
